column4: The identical frame لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا ٱلْإِنسَانَ replaces the section's bodily kebed with “the best proportion,” directly confirming its upright, balanced reading.
God brings humans from their mothers' bellies knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts; the body and its faculties are expressly bestowed tools calling for gratitude.
Humanity is made from a mixed drop as a test and made hearing and seeing, joining bodily manufacture, endowed organs, and accountability in one claim.
After the organs and test of 76:2, God guides the way and the human becomes grateful or ungrateful, matching the section's question of which direction the given tools take.
“Created the human” begins a two-ayah sequence in which bodily creation is immediately followed by the gift of expression.
God “taught him البيان,” making articulate speech a created human capacity just as the section treats the tongue and lips as furnished instruments.
ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ names creation, proportioning, and balancing, the exact bodily senses developed from خلق and kebed.
God assembles the human in whatever form He wills, extending 82:7's image of a body deliberately fitted from parts.
God “created and proportioned,” a concise parallel to the section's complete and balanced human construction.
God measures and guides; following 87:2, this reproduces the section's sequence from fitted creation to directed use.
The womb contains a lump مُّخَلَّقَةٍ وَغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ, the very Qur'anic form behind the section's dictionary example of a fully formed piece of flesh.
The drop becomes clot, lump, bones clothed with flesh, then “another creation,” staging the craftsman-like, part-by-part making of the body.
God proportions the human, breathes into him, and makes hearing, sight, and hearts; formed body and usable faculties are one gift.
The addressee is reminded that God produced them and made hearing, eyes, and hearts, yet they give little thanks, directly posing the section's question about use of organs.
The hearing, sight, and hearts granted to a powerful people availed them nothing when they rejected God's signs, showing endowed tools failing through their use.
At judgment hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, turning the body's granted parts into witnesses of how they were used.
The condemned address their own skins and ask why they testified; the body's parts answer within the scene begun in 41:20.
They did not expect hearing, eyes, and skins to testify and thought God did not know much of what they did, directly reversing the section's man who thinks no one sees him.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify against their owners, so the speaking organ becomes accountable rather than remaining its owner's obedient instrument.
God seals their mouths while hands speak and feet testify; the boasting mouth is stopped and another bodily witness takes over.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each subject to questioning, explicitly stating the accountability of furnished faculties.
Moses asks God to untie a knot from his tongue, joining the physical speaking organ with the section's image of opening what is bound.
The requested result is that people understand Moses' قول, placing tongue and utterance together exactly as the section joins lisān and yaqūlu.
Moses says his chest tightens and his tongue does not move freely, bringing chest, tongue, and obstructed outward speech into one body.
Moses calls Aaron more fluent than himself in tongue and asks that he support his message, treating the tongue as the working tool of address.
Abraham confesses that the One who created him is the One who guides him, matching the section's creation-to-guidance sequence.
Abraham next says God feeds and gives him drink, completing the section's sequence from creation and guidance to the mouth's reception of provision.
At distribution, relatives, orphans, and the poor must be provided from the estate and addressed with a recognized good قول, commanding the mouth's material and verbal work together.
Dependants are to be fed and clothed from property and spoken to with a recognized good word, again pairing provision with responsible speech.
The covenant joins care for kin, orphans, and the needy with speaking good to people, directing resources and utterance toward others together.
A recognized good word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, judging what leaves the mouth alongside what the hand gives.
The righteous feed food they love to the needy, orphan, and captive, precisely realizing the turn from one's own appetite toward another mouth.
Their accompanying speech says they feed only for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, opposing the section's boastful utterance after spending.
When told to spend from God's provision, disbelievers answer aloud, “Should we feed” someone God could feed; their mouth uses speech to refuse another mouth food.
God is described as the One who feeds and is not fed, establishing the ultimate asymmetry behind the section's one person asking and another giving food.
Moses and his companion ask a town's people for food and are denied hospitality, directly enacting the dictionary relation in which one asks to be fed and another may give.
Expiation for spoken oaths includes feeding ten needy people or freeing a neck, uniting the section's mouth, food, and فك رقبة in one ayah.
A wrongful bodily declaration about one's wife is answered by freeing a neck before contact, turning harmful speech into a duty of release.
Whoever cannot free the neck must eventually feed sixty needy people, continuing the same correction from mouth-made wrong to another mouth's nourishment.
The accidental killer must free a believing neck, another direct Qur'anic instance of the emancipatory action named by فك رقبة.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to kin, orphans, needy people, travelers, beggars, and “the necks,” gathering feeding's social field and liberation.
Obligatory charity is assigned both to the poor and needy and to “the necks,” placing material relief and emancipation in the same distribution.
The relative, needy person, and traveler are to receive their due, directing owned provision outward rather than into boast or waste.
If one must turn from those claimants while awaiting provision, one must still speak an easy word to them, preserving the mouth's good outward work when it cannot give.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor wholly outspread, using two named body parts to measure miserliness and waste around 17:26–28.
The orphan must not be oppressed, directing power toward the same vulnerable figure whom the section commands one to feed.
The asker must not be repelled, governing the encounter between a needy person's requesting mouth and the addressee's response.
God's favor is to be spoken of, making speech a grateful use of what was given rather than a boast of personal expenditure.
The denier physically repels the orphan, the social and bodily reverse of opening one's means toward the vulnerable.
He does not urge the feeding of the poor, a direct parallel to refusal of the steep path's إطعام.
The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” opens a sequence contrasting possessive wealth-use with care for the vulnerable.
They do not urge one another to feed the needy, directly matching the mouth's failure to advocate food as well as to give it.
They consume inheritance in a devouring consumption, turning the eating mouth toward others' wealth rather than others' hunger.
Their excessive love of wealth explains the sequence's failure to honor and feed, illuminating the boast over amassed or expended المال.
The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him, reversing the confident mouth that boasts of what it did with a mass of wealth.
His cry هَلَكَ عَنِّى سُلْطَانِيَهْ turns the section's أَهْلَكْتُ boast into the loss of his own authority.
His punishment is explained by his failure to urge feeding the needy, making the absent outward word part of the failure to nourish.
He has no food except foul discharge, a punitive reversal of the nourishing food he would not direct to a poor mouth.
Only the sinners eat that food, identifying the receiving mouths and completing the punitive meal of 69:36.
Those in Saqar confess, “We did not feed the needy,” naming the failed inward use of food as a cause of judgment.
They add that they joined those who plunged into vain discourse, placing corrupt outward talk beside the refusal to feed in 74:44.
No قول is uttered without a watcher ready to record it, directly answering the speaker who thinks no one sees his boast.
People pass a rumor with their tongues and say with their mouths what they do not know, while deeming it slight though it is grave with God.
Hypocrites say with their mouths what is not in their hearts, separating the speaking instrument's output from inward truth.
Some say “we believe” with their mouths although their hearts have not believed, another explicit misuse of mouth-to-mouth profession.
The desert Arabs say with their tongues what is not in their hearts, exposing the tongue as a tool capable of divided direction.
Human social fictions are called “your saying with your mouths,” while God says truth and guides the way, opposing mouth-made claim to true قول and guidance.
A grave claim is described as a word coming out of their mouths, foregrounding the outward bodily passage and moral weight of speech.
A group twist their tongues with the Book so listeners mistake human distortion for revelation, a concrete wrong turning of the speaking organ.
The addressees must not let their tongues falsely label things lawful and unlawful, because that bodily utterance fabricates a lie against God.
Believers are commanded to speak a straight, sound قول, giving the section's tongue an explicitly right-directed outward task.
God commands His servants to say what is best because Satan can sow division between them, showing the interpersonal consequence of the mouth's direction.
“When you speak, be just,” even concerning a relative, subjects the organ's outward act to the same moral measure as property and covenant.
Avoidance of false قول is commanded beside avoidance of idols, giving speech a concrete boundary rather than treating it as neutral output.
God knows the treachery of eyes and what chests conceal, joining two enumerated bodily regions to the answer to “did no one see him?”
Whether speech is concealed or voiced, God knows what lies in breasts, directly relating mouth, hidden chest, and divine knowledge.
“Would the One who created not know?” grounds the knowledge of 67:13 in the Maker's intimate knowledge of the made body.
“Does he not know that God sees?” is the direct rhetorical answer to the section's self-assured man who supposes no one saw him.
ʿĀd boast aloud, “Who is stronger than us?” and are answered that their Creator is stronger, directly reversing imagined bodily power.
The passage begins with the slanderer and backbiter, a mouth turned toward injury before it turns to his relation with wealth.
That same person gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, joining corrupt utterance to possessive accumulation.
He supposes his wealth will make him immortal, exposing the same boastful delusion that bodily power and wealth escape their limit.
The garden owner says during direct conversation that he has more wealth and a stronger following, closely paralleling boast issued from a wealthy mouth.
Entering his garden, he says he does not think it will ever perish, making his spoken confidence in possession explicit.
His companion answers by recalling that God created him from dust and a drop and then proportioned him as a man, confronting wealth-boast with bodily making.
The companion supplies the right garden utterance—acknowledging God's will and that power belongs to God—against the owner's boast.
Qārūn is told to use what God gave for the lasting abode, do good as God did good to him, and not seek corruption, a direct rule for a bestowed resource's direction.
Qārūn replies that his wealth came by his own knowledge, but is reminded that God destroyed generations stronger than he, pairing mouth-boast with the limit of power.
The affluent say, “We are greater in wealth and children, and we will not be punished,” another explicit wealth-boast that presumes immunity.
The garden owners whisper that no needy person may enter upon them that day, using speech to shut their crop away from another mouth.
When the garden is ruined they say, “Rather, we are deprived,” making the would-be deprivers experience deprivation.
The most balanced among them recalls that he had urged them to glorify God, preserving a right spoken intervention inside the withholding scene.
The bodily act of frowning and turning away begins a rebuke over how one's face and attention are directed toward a vulnerable visitor.
The visitor is identified by his blindness, making an impaired bodily faculty central to the ethical encounter.
The self-sufficient person receives attention, reversing the section's demand that faculties and effort turn toward one in need.
The one who comes striving is the person whose approach should receive attention, correcting the body's social direction in 80:1.
The Prophet is told to keep with humble worshippers and not let his eyes pass beyond them seeking worldly adornment, directing sight away from wealth-status.
The Prophet must not extend his eyes toward others' worldly splendor; God's provision is better and more lasting, joining sight to the appraisal of provision.
Calling false gods is compared to one stretching hands toward water so it will reach his mouth, yet it never does, directly staging sought water and an unfilled mouth.
The river test distinguishes drinking from merely taking a handful, and uses يَطْعَمْهُ for tasting it, directly illustrating طعم as taste applied to water.
Moses reaches a water source crowded by people watering while two women hold back, closely realizing the section's secondary scene of heavily sought water.
Moses waters for the women and then declares his own need for whatever good God sends, turning competition at water into provision for another and a request for provision.
“Have you considered the water you drink?” makes the mouth's received water an occasion to recognize the giver.
God could make that water bitter, revealing the drink's dependence and the boundary on the drinker's access.
Every person's record is fastened to his neck and brought out as an open book, remarkably joining the section's neck with its dictionary image of unsealing a book.
The person is commanded to read his own book and suffice as his own reckoner, bringing the opened record through the mouth into self-accounting.
At death the departing life reaches the collarbones, placing human helplessness at the very bodily region evoked by the section's terāʾib gloss.
The reproductive fluid emerges from between backbone and تَرَائِب, the exact Qur'anic bodily sense of the root invoked through matraba.
أَصْحَابُ ٱلْمَيْمَنَةِ exactly repeats the section's title for the people of the right side and asks what their state will be.
أَصْحَابُ ٱلْيَمِينِ restates the same company through the right hand or right side, clarifying meymena's bodily orientation.
The person given his book in his right hand speaks and invites others to read it, combining right hand, mouth, and accountable record.
“Eat and drink pleasantly” is the reward announced in the right-hand recipient's scene, aligning the mouth's reception with prior deeds.
Receiving one's book in the right hand marks the bodily side as the sign of a favorable reckoning.
The people of the right are excepted from pledged captivity and question the guilty, preserving the right-side designation outside surah 90.
God's opening or expansion of the Prophet's chest gives direct Qur'anic bodily content to the section's secondary “balad as chest.”
Guidance is pictured as God expanding a chest for surrender, while misguidance makes it tight and constricted, turning the chest in two opposed directions.
People fold their chests to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and reveal, joining a body part to the failure of imagined invisibility.
The hearers are directed to signs “in yourselves,” inviting the made body itself to answer the section's catalogue of organs.
God forms humans in wombs however He wills, presenting prenatal bodily shaping as deliberate divine work.
Humans are created in their mothers' wombs, creation after creation in three darknesses, extending the image of a body made stage by stage.
The drop becomes a clot and God creates and proportions it, another direct sequence of bodily material and measured making.
From that made body God produces the male and female pair, completing the creation sequence of 75:37–38.
The human is created from a lowly fluid, recalling the material out of which the complete, upright body is made.
The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, identifying the womb as the workshop-like enclosure of bodily formation.
It remains there until a known measure, making bodily development a timed and fitted process.
God says “We measured,” then praises the measurers, closing the scene on deliberate proportion rather than self-made power.
The addressee is made to consider the reproductive fluid he emits, beginning a challenge about who actually fashions the body.
“Do you create it, or are We the creators?” directly overturns the human's illusion of autonomous bodily power.
The human supposes God will not assemble his bones, making dismembered bodily parts the object of his doubt.
God answers that He can proportion even the fingertips, an especially fine-grained craftsman image of reconstructing the body.
Though created from a drop, the human becomes an open disputant, juxtaposing made body and boastful mouth.
He voices a parable about decayed bones and forgets his own creation, making wrong speech arise from forgetfulness of bodily making.
The commanded answer says the One who originated the bones will revive them, restoring the Maker's power over every part.
God creates the human from a drop, yet the human becomes a manifest disputant, the same turn from dependent body to self-asserting speech.
Those who wrongfully consume orphans' property are only eating fire into their bellies, reversing food's nourishing entry and the duty toward the orphan.
The punished have no food except a bitter thorn, a meal that inverts the section's life-giving food offered in hunger.
That food neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, explicitly denying the two functions that make feeding another mouth merciful.
The arrogant are given putrid water to drink, turning the sought drink of the mouth into punishment.
The drinker tries to gulp it but can scarcely swallow, a precise reversal of the opened throat through which provision should enter.
The tree of Zaqqūm is called the food of the sinner, making food itself carry judgment.
That food is like molten substance boiling in bellies, turning the body's interior from recipient of nourishment into a site of torment.
Paradise's unspoiled drink is opposed to boiling water that cuts intestines, setting a bodily boundary between provision and punitive ingestion.
What misers withhold will be collared around their necks at resurrection, joining hoarded wealth to the very body part liberation should free.
Combat begins with striking necks and binding captives before release or ransom, the violent and captive boundary against which “freeing a neck” signifies mercy.
Shackles rise to the disbelievers' necks and force their heads upward, turning the upright neck from a free bodily posture into constraint.
After the best bodily proportion of 95:4, humanity is reduced to the lowest of the low, exposing the made form's vulnerability and moral limit.
The person who makes desire his god has hearing and heart sealed and a covering over sight, a judgmental reversal of the organs first bestowed.
God can take hearing and sight and seal hearts, making explicit that bodily faculties are contingent gifts rather than owned powers.
People have hearts, eyes, and ears but do not use them for understanding, seeing, or hearing, the clearest reversal of properly directed bodily tools.
Moses asks for his chest to be expanded before asking for the tongue's knot to be untied; the bodily prayer coheres with the section's chest-and-mouth inventory.
One ayah surveys creation from dust, drop, clot, childhood, maturity, and old age, supporting the section's made body through its successive completed states.
God created humans and made their forms beautiful, then names return to Him, linking finished bodily form with accountability.
Hell's drink is like molten liquid that scalds faces, a specific contrary image in which bringing drink to the mouth destroys the visible body.
Pilgrims are told to eat sacrificial animals and feed the distressed poor, giving the mouth both reception and outward provision in one command.
The worshippers may eat from the sacrificial camels and feed both the contented and the petitioner, again dividing food between one's own mouth and others.
People may eat harvest fruit but must give its due and avoid waste, placing personal consumption beside another's material claim.
God feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, naming feeding as a divine gift that humans are then called to extend.
God says He seeks neither provision nor feeding from creatures, setting the dependent human mouth against the self-sufficient giver.
God is the provider and possessor of firm power, grounding the asymmetry in 51:57 and the section's supplied bodily tools.
The disciples ask whether a table can be sent from heaven, staging spoken request for a shared source of food.
They say they want to eat from the table so their hearts are reassured, making the mouth's inward act the desired confirmation.
Jesus asks God to send the table as a feast, sign, and provision, joining prayerful speech to divinely given food.
Joseph's brothers say hardship has touched them and ask for full measure and charity, a concrete hungry mouth addressing one able to provide.
Private speech is mostly without good unless it commands charity, recognized good, or reconciliation, directing talk toward material and social benefit.
Charity is required before private consultation with the Messenger, placing a material act before the privilege of spoken exchange.
Those who spend without following their gift with reminders or injury preserve reward, clarifying the giving-and-speech measure stated in 2:263.
Believers are told not to nullify charity with reminders and injury, showing harmful output undoing the value of outward provision.
Wealth and children do not bring one near to God; faith and right action do, correcting the immunity-boast spoken in 34:35.
“Everything is perishing except His face” gives هالك its absolute sense and places the boast of expended wealth within what cannot remain.
Everyone upon the earth passes away, a nonfinancial use of the destruction root that strips bodily possession of permanence.
The majestic face of the Lord remains after 55:26's universal passing, fixing the boundary between made body and enduring Maker.
The Prophet is told not to obey a habitual swearer, beginning a portrait of a mouth repeatedly turned to corrupt output.
The same figure is a slanderer who circulates malicious speech, specifying the tongue's interpersonal harm.
He actively hinders good, transgresses, and sins, connecting the wrong-speaking figure to blocked benefit for others.
His wealth and children explain his presumption, joining the corrupt mouth of 68:10–11 to confidence in possessions.
Hostile people please believers with their mouths while their hearts refuse, a vivid mouth-to-mouth address divided from inward stance.
Hatred has appeared from enemies' mouths while their breasts conceal more, showing speech emerging from and partially exposing the body's interior.
Opponents seek to extinguish God's light with their mouths, assigning destructive intention to the same bodily outlet made for speech.
The repeated attempt to extinguish God's light with mouths gives a second direct image of speech used against revelation.
Rejecting peoples put their hands to their mouths and verbally deny their messengers, combining bodily gesture and resistant speech.
Those unable to find transport leave with eyes overflowing in grief because they lack something to spend, turning sight and absent wealth toward sincere need.
A chest expanded for surrender stands in God's light, giving the secondary chest image a spiritual orientation toward guidance.
The dying person may be among the people of the right, carrying the right-side classification into the body's final passage.
A greeting of peace is addressed to that person “from the people of the right,” adding beneficent speech to the right-side scene.
The addressee must consider who could bring flowing water if their water sank away, exposing the hidden dependence behind every mouthful.
The human is asked what deceived him concerning his generous Lord, introducing 82:7–8's reminder that this Lord created, balanced, and assembled his body.
God places the reproductive drop in a secure lodging, supplying the womb-stage immediately before the lump, bones, and flesh of 23:14.
God produces humans and gives them hearing, eyes, and hearts, yet they give little thanks, directly treating organs as bestowed and answerable faculties.
God forms humans and makes their forms beautiful, then provides good things, joining bodily craftsmanship to what enters and sustains the made body.
The oath turns to the self and the One who proportioned it, an inward counterpart to the section's upright, balanced bodily making.
The fashioned self is inspired with both its wrong and its piety, a precise nonbodily parallel to endowed human capacity taking one of two directions.
The command to recite in the name of the creating Lord joins an outward act of the mouth to acknowledgment of the Maker.
God creates the human from a clinging clot, grounding the reciting person of 96:1 in bodily dependence.
The human transgresses, beginning the exact posture of self-assertion that culminates in the reminder that God sees in 96:14.
His transgression arises because he sees himself as self-sufficient, closely paralleling the section's imagined immunity from another's power or sight.
God created the human, knows the self's whisper, and is nearer than the jugular vein, making bodily intimacy the answer to imagined concealment.
A husband's bodily comparison of his wife to his mother's back is condemned as an objectionable falsehood, the harmful mouth-act corrected by freeing and feeding in 58:3–4.
Backbiting is pictured as eating the flesh of one's dead brother, fusing the mouth's outward injury and inward eating into one repellent reversal.
Believers are asked why they say what they do not do, directly making utterance answerable to action.
God greatly hates saying what one does not do, completing 61:2's judgment of irresponsible output from the mouth.
Cowards assail believers with sharp tongues while greedy for benefit, joining injurious speech to acquisitive appetite in one bodily portrait.
Those who suppose God does not hear their secrets and private talk are told that His messengers record it, answering the boast spoken under imagined invisibility.
The Messiah and his mother both ate food; ordinary bodily intake proves their creaturely dependence despite exalted claims about them.
Giving and fearing God begin the path whose outcome is ease, directing possession outward rather than treating it as grounds for boast.
The one who is miserly and regards himself as self-sufficient embodies the reverse direction of both feeding another and remembering one's made dependence.
The most reverent person gives wealth to purify himself, a deliberate right use of property against the image of boastful expenditure.
The faithful recognize an assigned right in their wealth, making provision something already oriented beyond its possessor.
That right belongs to the asker and the deprived, identifying both the requesting mouth and the need that another person's resources must answer.
The righteous acknowledge in their wealth a right for the asker and the deprived, a direct counterimage to wealth spoken of as one's private feat.
Hidden needy people refrain from importunate asking and may be mistaken for self-sufficient, requiring perception rather than waiting for a hungry mouth to insist.
Care for relatives, orphans, needy people, neighbors, travelers, and dependants is set against the arrogant boaster whom God does not love.
The miserly both withhold and command others to withhold while concealing God's bounty, misdirecting possession and outward speech together.
Pure milk comes for drinkers from within cattle bellies between waste and blood, making an inward body region the workshop of mouth-ready provision.
Livestock bellies yield drink, while the animals also supply many benefits and food, joining bodily interior, drinking, and eating as provision.
Twelve springs gush from the struck stone, every group knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink God's provision without corruption.
The repeated twelve-spring scene assigns each tribe its watering place and commands eating from good provision, ordering many mouths around supplied water.
God sends water in due measure, lodges it in the earth, and declares His ability to remove it, exposing every drinking mouth's dependence on measured provision.
God sends fertilizing winds and water from heaven for people to drink while they are not its storekeepers, sharply distinguishing giver from recipient.
The question asks whether humans sent drinking water down from the clouds or God did, identifying the provider between 56:68's drink and 56:70's threatened bitterness.
The human is commanded to look at his food, turning bodily sight toward reflection on what the mouth receives.
The long account of rain, split earth, crops, and fruit culminates in provision for humans and their livestock, locating a meal within divine preparation.
Those given their record in their right hands read it, joining right hand, opened book, and the mouth's act of reading.
God knows the Prophet's chest is constricted by what hostile people say, tracing painful outward speech into a bodily interior.
The ayah says bodily eyes do not become blind; rather, hearts within chests do, distinguishing possession of an organ from its right perceptive use.
Believing men are commanded to lower their gaze, giving the endowed eyes a concrete disciplined direction.
The Prophet's sight neither swerved nor transgressed at the vision, presenting exact and bounded use of the eye.
Abraham asks for “a tongue of truth” among later people, extending lisān from the bodily speaking organ to enduring truthful repute.
Abraham and his family are granted mercy and an exalted “tongue of truth,” repeating the nonphysical outcome produced by truthful remembrance and speech.
Differences in human languages and colors are signs of God, placing tongues or languages within the deliberately varied made body.
The departing life reaches the throat while human onlookers stand helpless, making the mouth's bodily passage a scene of lost control.
God is nearer to the dying person than the watchers, though they cannot see, reversing the supposition that unseen presence means no one witnesses.
The hearers are challenged to return the departing life if they are truthful, exposing the hard limit on human power over the body.
The human is asked from what God created him, confronting pride by returning attention to bodily material.
God creates him from a drop and proportions him, directly naming the fitting of the finished body.
The human is asked to remember that God created him before he was anything, a direct correction of made humanity's self-sufficiency.
The human was a drop of emitted fluid, supplying the bodily material that God creates and proportions in 75:38.
God says He apportioned death among humans and cannot be outstripped, setting the Maker's power against bodily confidence.
God can replace humans with their likes and produce them in forms they do not know, extending bodily workmanship beyond the present form.
People ask aloud whether they will be raised after becoming bones and fragments, joining decayed bodily parts with disputing speech.
The answer identifies the One who originated them the first time, while their own mouths ask who will restore them.
Turning one's cheek from people and walking arrogantly are forbidden because God does not love the proud boaster, placing pride visibly in the body.
Measured walking and a lowered voice are commanded together, directing bodily posture and mouth-produced sound toward restraint.
The arrogant walker can neither split the earth nor equal mountains in height, exposing the limits of the upright body that displays pride.
“Your Lord is ever watchful” states the direct boundary on the section's belief that no one sees.
Pharaoh publicly proclaims his kingdom and flowing rivers and asks his people whether they see, combining boastful mouth, possession, and manipulated sight.
Qārūn's treasure keys burden a company of strong men, establishing the mass of wealth and bodily strength answered by his boast in 28:78.
The people of the left are named immediately opposite the people of the right, defining meymena's moral and spatial boundary.
The person given his book in his left hand speaks regretfully, reversing the right-hand recipient's confident invitation to read in 69:19.
The astray are told they will eat from the tree of Zaqqūm, turning the mouth's inward work into punishment.
They fill their bellies from Zaqqūm, making bodily fullness itself the reverse of merciful nourishment.
They then drink boiling water over the punitive food, completing a meal in which both inward acts of the mouth harm the body.
Collars are placed around necks and the condemned are dragged in chains, a bodily reversal of releasing a neck.
The condemned wealth-boaster is seized and shackled, turning imagined personal power into bodily capture.
He is inserted into a long chain, completing the restraint that stands opposite freeing another person's neck.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, adding the elemental material behind the later part-by-part body.
Creation from dust and a drop proceeds to pairs and wombs whose pregnancies God knows, joining bodily material, formation, and divine knowledge.
God's creation of humans from dust precedes their spreading as living people, a concise transition from base material to completed bodies.
Faith and good deeds are excepted from 95:5's lowering after beautiful proportion, showing that bodily form reaches its proper outcome through action.
The response to a question about spending directs good wealth to parents, kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, specifying the outward destination of possession.
People do not attain true goodness until they spend from what they love, setting the relinquishment of prized possession against boast over wealth.
The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need, a specific reversal of letting one's appetite or possession close against another.
People invited to spend in God's path may become miserly, and their miserliness turns back upon themselves.
Those unable to fast have a compensating duty of feeding a needy person, making another mouth's food the concrete substitute for a bodily act of restraint.
Humans may eat and drink but must not be excessive, placing a moral measure on the mouth's inward work.
Messengers are commanded to eat good things and do right, coupling bodily intake with the action expected from its recipients.
The hearers must eat lawful good provision and thank God for His favor, turning received food toward gratitude.
Believers are likewise commanded to eat good provision and thank God, a repeated formulation of responsible reception.
Abraham quietly brings a fat calf to his guests, staging food offered from one person toward other mouths.
He places the food near them and asks whether they will eat, joining offered provision and face-to-face speech.
Israel voices dissatisfaction with one food and asks Moses for earthly varieties, showing appetite directing speech despite existing provision.
A person's speech about worldly life can impress while his heart is fiercely hostile, distinguishing attractive mouth-output from inward stance.
When the ignorant address the servants of the Merciful, they answer with peace, giving mouth-to-mouth exchange a restrained direction.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are called guided, placing reception and selection of قول within the path of right use.
